lesson.title: Capstone: Design a Segmented, Defended Network From Scratch
lesson.summary: This capstone has you design a complete network for a small but realistic organization, choosing VLAN segmentation, subnet boundaries, and layered firewall rules that together enact defense in depth rather than leaning on any single control.
lesson.body:
This project is different in shape from the others: there is no code to run at the end, only a design, and a design has to be defensible on paper. Given a scenario, for example a small company with an office network, a guest wifi network, a set of internal servers, and some remote employees, produce a full network design: a diagram, an addressing plan, a VLAN plan, and a firewall rule set, along with a written explanation of why each piece exists.

The temptation is to start by drawing boxes and connecting them with lines. Resist it. Start instead from the assets and the trust levels involved. What data or systems actually matter most here, a customer database, say. Who legitimately needs to reach it, and from where. Only once you have honestly answered those questions should you start drawing VLAN boundaries and assigning subnets, because a design built the other way around tends to produce boundaries that look reasonable on a diagram but do not actually correspond to anything worth protecting.

VLANs are the tool for segmenting one physical network into separate logical broadcast domains, even when everything is plugged into the same physical switches. Put guest wifi on its own VLAN, with its own subnet sized appropriately by choosing the right subnet mask for the number of devices it actually needs to support, not an oversized block handed out out of habit. A firewall rule attached to that VLAN should allow only outbound internet access and explicitly block any path from the guest network into the employee or server VLANs. Put the internal servers on their own VLAN as well, reachable only from the specific employee or application subnets that genuinely need them, and only on the specific ports those services actually use, for example allowing the database port only from the application server subnet, not from every employee laptop on the office network. Devices like badge readers or security cameras, often poorly maintained and rarely patched, belong on their own VLAN too, so that even if one of them is compromised, it cannot reach anything sensitive.

None of this should rest on a single control, and that is the idea behind defense in depth. The firewall rules between VLANs are the primary control in this design, but a good design does not stop there. VLAN segmentation itself is a second, independent layer, since even a firewall misconfiguration does not automatically dissolve the VLAN boundary underneath it. Host level restrictions on the servers themselves form a third layer, so that even a device that somehow reaches the server VLAN still cannot connect to services it has no business touching. Logging and monitoring across these boundaries form a fourth layer, one that does not prevent an incident by itself but ensures one does not go unnoticed. The point of stacking these layers is that a single mistake, a misconfigured rule, a compromised device, a missed patch, should not be enough on its own to compromise the systems that matter most.

When you write up the final design, resist producing just a list of rules. For every VLAN boundary and every firewall rule, state plainly what it is protecting and against what. That discipline is what separates a design that merely looks secure from one that is actually reasoned through. This capstone is where subnetting arithmetic, VLAN tagging, firewall rule writing, and the general principle of defense in depth, each introduced somewhat separately earlier in the course, come together into the single kind of decision a real organization actually has to make about how it protects itself.
